opportunity: Acute Ischemic Stroke Code / Thrombolysis Coordination

checkpoints.title: 19. Why This Could Still Be an ART Opportunity

evidence.statement: The next discovery targets a high-consequence clinical workflow in a mid-scale Indian tertiary hospital:
> **Coordinating an acute ischemic stroke patient from emergency arrival through imaging, specialist assessment, thrombolysis eligibility decision and treatment initiation.**
The candidate hospital is **Baby Memorial Hospital (BMH), Kozhikode, Kerala**.

The hospital is currently described by its own website as having **490 operational beds**, including **100 ICU beds and 23 emergency-room beds**, with advanced diagnostic infrastructure and critical/emergency services.
A National Board of Examinations hospital profile lists Baby Memorial Hospital as a private hospital with **600 beds**.

This puts the hospital squarely within the intended mid-scale tertiary-hospital discovery boundary, although the discrepancy between installed/total and operational beds must be preserved rather than silently reconciled.
Acute ischemic stroke is an unusually strong ART discovery class because treatment eligibility can depend on a narrow time window and because the hospital workflow requires coordination across:

```text
EMERGENCY
   ↓
STROKE RECOGNITION
   ↓
NEUROLOGY
   ↓
IMAGING
   ↓
ELIGIBILITY ASSESSMENT
   ↓
THROMBOLYSIS
```
The Baby Memorial Hospital research team directly studied a mobile-app-based coordination strategy for this workflow.

```text
76 patients thrombolysed using the app
        ↓
Mean door-to-needle = 41 min
        ↓
89% treated within 60 min
        ↓
57% treated within 45 min
```

```text
100 prior patients
        ↓
Mean door-to-needle = 57 min
        ↓
67% within 60 min
        ↓
47% within 45 min
```
The mean door-to-needle reduction was **16 minutes**, and the difference was statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex and NIHSS score.

This is a potentially valuable discovery pattern because mature automation can expose the **next layer of manual exception work**.

- Baby Memorial Hospital is in Kozhikode, Kerala.
- Current BMH information reports 490 operational beds.
- NBE hospital profile reports 600 beds.
- BMH is a private tertiary-care hospital.

- Acute ischemic stroke thrombolysis is managed through Emergency Medicine and Neurology.
- BMH directly studied an app-based stroke workflow.
- The app supported patient parameters, NIHSS, checklist, dose calculation, team synchronization, notifications, patient movement and radiological image sharing.

- 76 patients were thrombolysed using the app.
- Mean DNT was 41 minutes.
- 89% were treated within 60 minutes.
- Historical comparison mean DNT was 57 minutes.
- 67% were treated within 60 minutes historically.
- Mean DNT reduction was 16 minutes.
- Difference was statistically significant after adjustment.

A 2024 quality-improvement project at Aster Medcity, Kochi independently reported mean door-to-needle time falling from 90.33 to 62.16 minutes after streamlining the stroke-code pathway, standardized protocols, symptom-onset/door-to-imaging/door-to-needle recording, staff education and direct neurology guidance.
This strongly supports the broader industry pattern.

- After first-generation digital coordination, residual exceptions may remain around patient movement, imaging and handoffs.
- A state-based exception layer could potentially address those residual gaps.
- ART could potentially sit above existing clinical systems rather than replacing them.

- BMH currently has residual manual stroke-code coordination work.
- Some delays still require human follow-up.
- Existing app functionality may not provide complete exception routing/escalation.
- ART could reduce residual coordination work.
- ART could create a more complete closed-loop exception record.

But the discovery must now pivot from:
> **"What coordination exceptions remain after BMH already implemented stroke-code automation?"**
That is the only defensible next question.

1. Is the 2017–2018 mobile app still used?
2. What replaced it, if anything?
3. Is it integrated with the current EHR?
4. Is imaging status automatically visible?
5. Is patient movement tracked digitally?

6. What still causes door-to-imaging delay?
7. What still causes imaging-to-review delay?
8. What still causes review-to-treatment delay?
9. Which delays require phone calls?
10. Which delays require nurses to manually chase people?

11. How many people touch a stroke-code case?
12. How many manual notifications occur?
13. How many follow-ups occur in delayed cases?
14. How often does escalation occur?
15. How much active time does a delayed case consume?

16. Which steps are safe to automate?
17. Which steps must remain clinical?
18. Which exception types are currently invisible?
19. Which existing automation cannot route/resolve?
20. What improvement would the hospital consider meaningful?

```text

> **OPP-001-01 identifies Baby Memorial Hospital, Kozhikode as a mid-scale Indian tertiary hospital and acute ischemic stroke-code/thrombolysis coordination as the discovery workflow. Direct BMH research demonstrated that a mobile-app-based coordination strategy supporting patient parameters, NIHSS, thrombolysis checklist, dose calculation, team synchronization, notifications, patient movement and radiological image sharing reduced mean door-to-needle time from 57 to 41 minutes in the studied comparison and increased the proportion treated within 60 minutes from 67% to 89%. The evidence therefore verifies a high-consequence, time-critical workflow and a historical coordination problem. However, BMH already implemented digital coordination, so the relevant ART question is the residual exception layer after that automation. Current 2026 residual manual work, automation limitations, active human effort and ROI remain UNKNOWN. ART Fit = MAYBE and Decision = VALIDATE.**
